"Indent" has several meanings depending on where it is used. Each meaning is related to the same core idea: pushing inward, creating a gap, or cutting into something.
Meaning 1: Moving text inward on a page (the most common modern use)

When you write or type, the left side of your text lines up along a straight, invisible vertical line called the margin. To indent means to start a particular line of text a little further to the right than that margin, creating a small empty gap at the very beginning of the line.

Think about the first line of a paragraph in a novel or an essay. It often starts a bit inside — not at the very edge like the other lines, but slightly pushed in. That small empty space at the start is called an indentation, and the action of creating it is called indenting.

When you press the Tab key on your keyboard, you are indenting. Writers use indentation to signal that a new paragraph is beginning. Programmers also indent lines of code to visually show that certain lines belong inside a block, a function, or a loop — it makes the structure of the code easier to read at a glance.
Meaning 2: Cutting or pressing into a surface to make a notch or dent

To indent also means to press into, cut into, or create a notch or dent on the edge or surface of something, making it uneven or jagged.

Imagine pressing your fingernail firmly into a bar of soap. The small hollow your nail leaves behind is an indentation. Similarly, imagine biting the edge of a piece of cardboard — those bite marks indent the edge.

So whenever something presses into a surface and leaves a visible mark, hollow, or jagged cut, we say the surface has been indented.
Meaning 3: Making an official order or requisition (mainly British and Commonwealth English)

In British English and the English used in countries like India, Australia, and Pakistan, "to indent" or "to indent for something" means to make a formal written order or request for goods or supplies — usually in a business, government, or military setting.

For example: "The army officer indented for winter clothing and new boots." This means the officer filled out an official request form to get those supplies. The document used to make such a request is called an indent.

This usage is less common in American English, where people would more typically say "to requisition" or "to place an order."
Meaning 4: Making two matching copies of a legal document (historical)

Centuries ago, when a legal agreement or contract was written between two parties, it was written out on a single piece of parchment and then cut along a wavy, zigzag, or serrated line to produce two separate pieces — one for each party.

Because the cut edges were completely unique and would only match each other perfectly, this method proved that both pieces genuinely came from the same original document and that neither had been tampered with. The verb for writing and cutting such a document was "to indent," and the resulting document was called an indenture. You may have heard this word in the context of indentured servants — workers who were legally bound by such a contract.

This is now a historical usage and you are unlikely to encounter it in everyday modern speech, but it is worth knowing because it ties all the meanings together.

Once you see the common thread, these meanings are easy to remember. Every sense of "indent" involves the idea of pushing inward, cutting into, or creating a gap:

  • In writing, you push the text inward from the margin.
  • On a surface, you press or cut inward to leave a mark.
  • In trade, you formally request something by filling in a specific document (historically tied to a notched or cut form).
  • In law, you literally cut a document into two jagged, matching pieces.

The noun form is "indent" or "indentation," and both simply refer to the gap, notch, or dent that is created by the act of indenting.
